name: Monarchism in France
summary: French monarchism is the family of movements that want France to be a monarchy again, with a hereditary king (or, for Bonapartists, emperor) as head of state in place of the Republic. Its strands disagree on almost everything else: Legitimists back the senior Bourbons and a Catholic, counter-revolutionary kingship; Orleanists back the House of Orleans and historically a liberal constitutional monarchy; Bonapartists back an imperial, plebiscitary dynasty. What they share is the dynastic principle, a head of state above party politics who embodies national unity and continuity, and attachment to France's historic institutions.
scope: The profile represents what the main strands of French monarchism share today and at their peak: Legitimists (Chambord's 1871 manifesto, the modern Legitimist circles), Orleanists (the 1830 Charter, Action Francaise, the left-wing Nouvelle Action Royaliste) and, more loosely, Bonapartists. Positions on which they split, such as democracy, parliament, economics, immigration, minorities and the place of the Church, are recorded as 0 or low confidence. The distinctive far-right doctrine of Maurras and Action Francaise is not the profile's basis; it is covered by integral-nationalism, and the Legitimist and Bonapartist strands by legitimists and bonapartism.

keyFigures.name: Charles Maurras
keyFigures.role: Leader of Action Francaise, the most influential twentieth-century royalist movement

sources.title: Manifeste du comte de Chambord, 5 juillet 1871
sources.author: Henri, comte de Chambord (extract published by Dalloz Etudiant)
sources.usedFor: Legitimist programme: decentralisation and local liberties, the king's principle and flag, rejection of privileges and feudal rights, national unity, Alsace-Lorraine, order and liberty.

sources.title: Charte constitutionnelle du 14 aout 1830
sources.author: Wikisource (text of the Orleanist constitution)
sources.usedFor: Orleanist constitutional monarchy: equality before the law, consent of the chambers to taxes, religious and press freedom, property, the king's executive power and command of the forces, shared lawmaking, peers.

sources.title: Monarchism in France
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.usedFor: The three strands, mostly constitutional aims, the Throne-and-Altar alliance, modern groups and their left-right placement, pretenders, the constitutional bar on changing the republican form.

sources.title: Orleanists
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.usedFor: Orleanism as the liberal, pro-business centre; the 1830 Charter; the July Monarchy; Action Francaise's and NAR's variants.

sources.title: Legitimists
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.usedFor: Counter-revolutionary views, Salic primogeniture and inalienable crown, Catholic king, Falloux law, Ultra-royalists, modern Legitimist organisations.

sources.title: Nouvelle Action Royaliste
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.usedFor: The left-wing Orleanist strand: democratic constitutional monarchy, Gaullism, Keynesian economics, souverainism, anti-Atlanticism, support for immigrant voting rights.

sources.title: Action Francaise
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.usedFor: The right-wing integral-royalist strand: anti-parliamentarism, federal monarchy, Catholicism as state religion, corporatism, nationalism, the 'four confederated states'.

sources.title: Bonapartism
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.usedFor: The Bonapartist strand as restoration of the House of Bonaparte and its style of government; scholarly disagreement over its definition.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: The strands split: NAR is Keynesian and anti-neoliberal, whereas Action Francaise wanted pay settled inside trade corporations rather than by statute.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Classic Orleanism was a pro-business liberal platform, but Action Francaise rejected economic liberalism and NAR opposes neoliberalism, so royalists are divided.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: The 1830 Charter only asks each to pay in proportion to wealth; beyond that the left-wing NAR and right-wing groups would answer differently.

unions-good.rationale: The July Monarchy repressed strikes and Action Francaise preferred corporations to class unions, but NAR sits with the Gaullist left; split.

property-fundamental.rationale: The 1830 Charter declares all property inviolable and allows expropriation only for a lawful public interest with prior compensation; the right-wing strands share this, NAR less emphatically.

cut-welfare.rationale: Nothing common to the strands; NAR's Keynesianism opposes cuts while right-wing royalists have no settled doctrine on welfare.

worker-ownership.rationale: No strand proposes it: Action Francaise's corporatism keeps firms privately owned and Orleanism was a property-owning bourgeois platform.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: NAR joined anti-racist campaigns with SOS Racisme, while Action Francaise's tradition is hostile to such laws; split.

strong-leader.rationale: Royalists want a king who can arbitrate above party conflict; NAR calls the Fifth Republic's strong presidency monarchical in inspiration and wants to extend it.

state-harmful.rationale: Every strand wants to restore a state with a king at its head; Chambord's manifesto offers to found with the French 'un gouvernement conforme aux besoins du pays'.

limit-guns.rationale: French royalist sources never treat gun ownership as an issue; no basis for either side.

decide-locally.rationale: Chambord's manifesto proposes to found the government on 'la decentralisation administrative et des franchises locales', and Action Francaise wanted a federal monarchy restoring provincial liberties; Orleanist and Bonapartist practice was more centralised. None of the cited sources takes up this question, so the answer is an inference.

rehabilitation.rationale: No royalist position on penal policy is documented across the strands.

traditional-family.rationale: Dynastic monarchy rests on family succession, and the Catholic Legitimist and Action Francaise strands make the family central; liberal Orleanists and NAR are less insistent. None of the cited sources takes up this question, so the answer is an inference.

more-religion-public.rationale: The royalist cause is bound up with the alliance of Throne and Altar and Legitimists require a Catholic king, though the Orleanist Charter guarantees equal freedom for all faiths. None of the cited sources takes up this question, so the answer is an inference.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Royalists treat the dynasty as national heritage: Chambord refused to give up the flag of Henri IV and Joan of Arc 'avec lui que s'est faite l'unite nationale'.

gradual-change.rationale: Orleanists were the liberal centre of gradual constitutional change, but Legitimists were counter-revolutionaries and Action Francaise aimed at a coup.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Both the left-wing NAR (souverainist, anti-Atlanticist) and the nationalist right of Action Francaise defend national sovereignty against supranational bodies.

free-trade.rationale: NAR is anti-neoliberal and Action Francaise rejected economic liberalism; no strand today champions free trade, though early Orleanists were pro-business.

nation-first.rationale: Action Francaise's integral nationalism and NAR's souverainism both put national sovereignty first; liberal Orleanists were less doctrinaire. None of the cited sources takes up this question, so the answer is an inference.

limit-growth.rationale: NAR has questioned growth models, but other strands have no position.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Climate policy is not a royalist issue; the strands give no basis for a shared answer.

revolution-justified.rationale: Legitimists are defined by counter-revolution, yet the Orleanist monarchy came from the 1830 revolution and Action Francaise planned a coup; split.

experts-over-public.rationale: Action Francaise distrusted popular opinion while NAR defends representative democracy; no shared view.

central-planning.rationale: Orleanists were pro-business and Action Francaise favoured corporatism over state planning; even NAR is Keynesian, not planner.

socialized-markets.rationale: Royalist strands keep private property (protected in the 1830 Charter) and none calls for worker or public ownership of all firms.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Action Francaise's corporatist and Catholic-social milieu leaned this way; Orleanist business liberals did not.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: No strand, from liberal Orleanists to corporatists, envisages abolishing money; the Charter guarantees property.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Action Francaise's corporatism supports it, but Orleanist liberalism and NAR's Keynesianism do not; split.

one-party-rule.rationale: Royalists want a king above parties, not a ruling party, and NAR backs representative democracy.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Restoring a monarchy is what defines the movement; Chambord's manifesto affirms 'mon principe' and asks France to call its king back.

democracy-best.rationale: Legitimists and Action Francaise opposed democracy, but NAR calls itself democratic; most royalists put the crown above elections.

direct-votes.rationale: The Orleanist Charter relies on elected chambers and Action Francaise distrusted popular votes; Bonapartist plebiscites are the exception.

workers-councils.rationale: No strand proposes councils; royalists base power on the crown with either chambers (Charter) or corporations (Action Francaise).

political-violence-never.rationale: Action Francaise had its street-fighting Camelots and coup plans, while NAR runs candidates in elections; split.

war-builds-character.rationale: No royalist doctrine on war's effect on national character.

separate-church-state.rationale: The Throne-and-Altar tradition, Legitimists' Catholic king and Action Francaise's call for Catholicism as state religion all reject strict separation; Orleanist pluralism softens it. None of the cited sources takes up this question, so the answer is an inference.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Even Catholic royalists want law grounded in tradition and the Church, not scripture; the Charter is secular in its legal basis.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Justice and command of the forces belong to the crown (Charter arts. 12-13); privatising them is foreign to every strand.

military-superiority.rationale: Patriotic royalists support defence, but no strand seeks superiority over rivals; NAR is anti-Atlanticist rather than militarist.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Royalists credit dynasty, faith and national history, and Action Francaise opposed Marxism outright.

equal-outcomes.rationale: A hereditary monarchy accepts inherited rank; even the left-wing NAR seeks the common good rather than equal outcomes.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: Not a royalist issue; no basis for a shared answer.

civilizational-union.rationale: Souverainist royalists defend the French nation-state over wider unions.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Catholic and Action Francaise royalists put duties first, though NAR defends the 1789 rights of man.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: No strand rejects industry; Orleanism was the party of financiers and business.

restore-past-order.rationale: Restoring the monarchy is by definition restoring a lost institution, and Legitimists are counter-revolutionary; but Orleanists and NAR want a modern monarchy compatible with 1789. None of the cited sources takes up this question, so the answer is an inference.

direct-action.rationale: Action Francaise historically favoured street action and a coup, while NAR and today's royalist parties stand in elections.

means-match-ends.rationale: Royalists have disputed tactics (coup versus elections) but never framed the question this way, so there is no basis for a side.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Royalists aim to restore a historic state and its institutions; abandoning civilisation contradicts the whole project.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Royalist thought is built on orders, trades and professions (Action Francaise's corporations), not their abolition.

distribute-by-need.rationale: No royalist strand is communist; the Charter protects property and Action Francaise opposed Marxism.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Action Francaise and Orleanists rejected Marxist analysis; NAR is Keynesian rather than Marxist.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Royalists seek rule by a king above classes, the opposite of class dictatorship.

collective-farming.rationale: The Charter guarantees property and Legitimism's rural base was small and large landowners; no strand favours collectivisation.

taxation-theft.rationale: The 1830 Charter requires every Frenchman to contribute to public expenses in proportion to his wealth; taxation is treated as a civic duty.

harm-principle.rationale: Catholic and traditionalist royalists accept moral legislation; liberal Orleanists less so.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Action Francaise stressed families, provinces and corporations, while NAR backs the 1789 rights of man; majority leans communitarian.

media-academia-power.rationale: Action Francaise denounced cultural elites, but this is not shared by the other strands.

organic-representation.rationale: Action Francaise and Legitimists wanted representation by families, provinces and trades, but the Orleanist Charter has elected deputies and NAR backs representative democracy.

total-state.rationale: Chambord promised decentralisation and local liberties, and the Charter guarantees religious and press freedom; no strand wants a total state.

national-rebirth.rationale: Royalists present the restoration as a remedy for the Republic's failings, Action Francaise most strongly; NAR is less apocalyptic.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Chambord's manifesto dismisses talk of 'droits feodaux' as phantoms raised in bad faith; royalists want a national king, not feudal bonds.

bound-labor.rationale: Chambord explicitly rejected the return of tithes and feudal rights as phantoms; no strand wants serfdom.

single-common-good.rationale: Royalists want a king above factions serving the common good; NAR's Renouvin frames monarchy as a means to the common good.

economic-freedom.rationale: Orleanist liberals tied political and economic liberty; Action Francaise did not.

rule-by-example.rationale: Royalists value the king's example but also law and charter; no settled view.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: Right-wing royalists might agree, but NAR campaigned for immigrant rights; split.

class-collaboration.rationale: Action Francaise's corporatism unites employers and workers, and royalists see the king as above classes; NAR's Gaullism also favours cooperation.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Royalists treat inherited symbols and institutions as sacred trusts, as Chambord did with the white flag.

workers-nation.rationale: Not a royalist issue except in Action Francaise's nationalism.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Legitimists keep Salic male succession to the throne, but no strand sets out wider legal gender roles.

ban-interest.rationale: Orleanism was backed by financiers; no strand proposes a ban.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: No royalist strand proposes racial segregation; NAR is explicitly anti-racist.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Royalists see the crown as above classes, the opposite of the Marxist view of the state.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: Energy production is not a royalist theme; only NAR's Gaullist interest in national independence touches it, without a stated view.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Nationalist royalists expect assimilation, but NAR's anti-racist stance differs; split.

elite-replacement.rationale: Some on the royalist far right hold such views, but NAR and Orleanist liberals reject them.

national-mission.rationale: No royalist doctrine of exporting a form of government.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Action Francaise rallied opposition to a Republic it saw as corrupt, and royalists generally criticise the republican political class; NAR is milder.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: No royalist strand addresses accountability for past security-force abuses; left and right royalists would differ.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The 1830 Charter opens 'Les Francais sont egaux devant la loi', Chambord disowned any return of privileges, and NAR upholds the 1789 Declaration.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Legitimists backed the Falloux law restoring the Church's role in education; liberal strands differ.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Louis-Philippe was made king by the chambers and NAR is democratic, but Legitimists base legitimacy on inherited right; split.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Royalists want a state with armed forces and coercive law under the crown; libertarian non-aggression is foreign to them.

separated-powers.rationale: The Orleanist Charter divides executive power (the king) from lawmaking shared with two chambers, though Action Francaise wanted the king to reign and govern.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: Council-house sales are a British policy question no French royalist strand has addressed.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: The Orleanist Charter forbids the king to suspend laws, while Action Francaise envisaged an authoritarian transition; split.

party-controls-media.rationale: The Charter declares that censorship can never be re-established, and royalists reject party rule; Action Francaise was less liberal.

party-commands-army.rationale: The Charter gives command of the armed forces to the king, not any party.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: NAR urged a no vote on the 2005 European Constitution and is souverainist; Action Francaise is nationalist.

head-commands-forces.rationale: The 1830 Charter gave the king executive power and command of the land and sea forces, and Legitimists wanted a governing king, but Nouvelle Action Royaliste wants a parliamentary monarchy; the royalist tradition leans toward a commanding king.

clerical-rule.rationale: Royalists want a lay king allied with the Church, not rule by clergy.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Royalist patriotism runs the other way: some monarchists joined the Resistance out of patriotic concern.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: The Charter bans censorship, but the Catholic right is more willing; split.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Royalists want a hereditary head, so presidential terms are secondary; NAR criticised the five-year term.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: NAR's anti-Atlanticism points to leaving NATO, other strands differ.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Legitimism had a rural base, but this is not a doctrine of the family.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: France is not a nation divided by an outside power, so royalism offers no position on this.

death-penalty.rationale: The Ultra-royalists made sacrilege a capital crime, but modern left royalists would not back executions; split.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: Third-world debt is not a royalist issue; NAR's left economics might favour relief, the right would not.

constituent-assembly.rationale: A restoration needs constitutional change, and the royalist majority of 1871 was an elected assembly; but Legitimists hold the king's right does not come from an assembly.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Royalists want a hereditary head of state; in Legitimist law the crown passes automatically to the heir on the king's death, leaving nothing to elect.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: The Charter treats property as inviolable, Catholic and corporatist royalists subordinate it to the common good; split.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: A Marxist debate about the Soviet Union in which royalists take no part.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: The Throne-and-Altar alliance and Legitimist Catholicism oppose curbing the Church; Orleanists were more Gallican.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: A hereditary king above party politics as a symbol of unity is the core case all strands make; NAR presents the monarch as embodying the common good.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Legitimists keep the Catholic sacred kingship, but Orleanists and NAR see a constitutional monarch; split.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: The Charter bars the king from suspending laws or dispensing from them, though the Ultra-royalists opposed limits on royal power. None of the cited sources takes up this question, so the answer is an inference.

mixed-constitution.rationale: The Charter combines a king, appointed (possibly hereditary) peers and elected deputies; Action Francaise would put more weight on the king.

leader-cult.rationale: Royalists honour the dynasty, but mass praise is not part of the tradition; split.

land-redistribution.rationale: The Charter protects property, including land sold off in the Revolution, against seizure.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: The Charter states that each professes his religion with equal freedom; no modern royalist group seeks penalties.

moral-incentives.rationale: Socialist work incentives are outside royalist debate; Catholic duty and private enterprise pull different ways.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Royalists reject revolutionary vanguards; Action Francaise's coup plans were a restoration, not revolution.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Royalists defend a hereditary crown and the Charter allowed hereditary peerages, but Chambord disowned any return of 'privileges'. None of the cited sources takes up this question, so the answer is an inference.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: France has no racial preferences in admissions or hiring, so the question does not arise in royalist debate.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: A forecast about capitalism that no royalist strand makes; their critiques of liberalism concern its morals, not its collapse.

delink-world-market.rationale: A dependency-theory prescription royalists do not discuss; NAR's souverainism stops short of it.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: The Orleanist Charter and NAR's support for the 1789 Declaration favour written rights, Action Francaise did not; split.

elective-rulers.rationale: Legitimists hold the crown inalienable and passed by Salic primogeniture, and Chambord claimed the throne by his 'principe'; royalists reject choosing the ruler by election.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Orleanists came to power in 1830 by removing Charles X for breaking the Charter, while Legitimists reject that right; split. None of the cited sources takes up this question, so the answer is an inference.

parliament-supreme.rationale: The Charter shares lawmaking between the king and two chambers, and Action Francaise was anti-parliamentary; no strand makes parliament supreme.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Animal ethics is outside royalist doctrine.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: A critical-theory claim royalists do not make; Action Francaise blamed democracy, not mass culture, for decline.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: A Gramscian claim that royalists neither adopt nor discuss.

party-own-road.rationale: A question internal to communist parties, which royalists reject altogether.

return-lost-territory.rationale: Chambord's 1871 manifesto invoked lost Alsace and Lorraine; no modern claims.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: Some monarchists joined the Resistance while Action Francaise welcomed Vichy; split.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: Royalists are divided by their Second World War history (Resistance versus Vichy), and none states this equivalence.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: An American historical question outside French royalist debate.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: The 1830 Charter provides that no tax may be levied unless both chambers consent; Action Francaise gave assemblies less weight.

single-official-language.rationale: Decentralist royalists favour regional languages, but French is the national language; split.

corporate-influence.rationale: Orleanists were backed by financiers, while NAR is anti-neoliberal; split.

job-guarantee.rationale: Keynesian NAR might support it, others not; split.

industrial-unions.rationale: Union structure is not a royalist question; Action Francaise preferred trade corporations to either form.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: Action Francaise denounced the 'four confederated states' of Jews, Protestants, Freemasons and foreigners, but Orleanist liberals and the anti-racist NAR reject such views.

informal-organisation.rationale: Royalists organise in standing associations and parties such as NAR and the Legitimist circles.

national-law-over-international.rationale: Souverainism is shared by NAR and the nationalist right of Action Francaise.

religious-nation.rationale: Legitimists require a Catholic king, but the Orleanist Charter grants equal religious freedom and NAR is secular-democratic; split.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: The Charter protects all property, means of production included; royalists reject common ownership.

defeat-communism.rationale: Action Francaise opposed Marxism; NAR is not anti-communist in this sense.

religion-illusion.rationale: Royalism is bound to the Throne-and-Altar tradition and Legitimists require a Catholic king; Maurras's agnosticism was an exception.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: Orleanists embraced commerce, Action Francaise rejected liberal capitalism; split.

treaties-binding.rationale: Treaties with internal nations are not a French royalist question.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Action Francaise sought a corporatist third way, but Orleanists were pro-business liberals; split.

historical-land-claim.rationale: Chambord's manifesto addresses Alsace-Lorraine, but strands differ and no shared line on historic claims exists.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: Legitimists, rooted in Catholic tradition, would lean to yes while Orleanists and the left-wing NAR would not; the strands split.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Legitimists and Action Francaise favour a Catholic state religion while Orleanists and NAR do not.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Not a shared issue; Bonapartists were imperial while the Charter and NAR are silent on colonies.

participatory-democracy.rationale: NAR is democratic but Action Francaise and Legitimists are anti-parliamentarian; the strands split.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: A head of state above party appeals across left and right, but adherents themselves place strands on both sides.

islam-incompatible.rationale: Strands split: Legitimists and Action Francaise are suspicious of Islam while NAR backed immigrant voting rights.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Legitimists hold a Catholic kingship by divine right while Orleanists rest on the 1830 Charter and the chambers. None of the cited sources takes up this question, so the answer is an inference.

religious-dress-in-state.rationale: French laicite is a republican norm and the strands split on the Church's place in the state.

social-market-economy.rationale: Orleanism is pro-business and liberal while NAR is Keynesian and Action Francaise corporatist; the strands split.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: The Charter gives the king command of the forces, and the strands treat the crown as embodying national continuity and defence.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: NAR was anti-Atlanticist and Gaullist while other strands had no line on blocs; the strands split.

dynastic-succession.rationale: The dynastic principle is what defines the strands: Legitimists hold Salic primogeniture and an inalienable crown, Orleanists and Bonapartists hold hereditary dynasties.

refuse-lender-austerity.rationale: The strands split: the sovereigntist, anti-Atlanticist NAR would refuse, whereas the pro-business Orleanist tradition accepts lender terms.

property-franchise.rationale: Historic Orleanism used a tax-based franchise under the 1830 Charter, while the modern NAR favours democratic suffrage, so the strands split.

press-owned-by-wealth.rationale: Orleanists defended press freedom in the Charter while the NAR criticises money power; Action Francaise had its own press; adherents split.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: The 1830 Charter set equality before the law and the king's role under fixed law, and Chambord's manifesto speaks of order and liberty; Bonapartist plebiscitary rule is a partial exception. None of the cited sources takes up this question, so the answer is an inference.

racial-franchise.rationale: The Charter's equality before the law and the NAR's support for immigrant voting rights point against racial limits, though Action Francaise's nationalism is more exclusionary. None of the cited sources takes up this question, so the answer is an inference.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Every strand rejects state atheism: Legitimists defend Catholic kingship and the others accept the Church's place in French history, as the Chambord manifesto and Charter's religious clauses show.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: The Napoleonic Code placed wives under husbands' authority and Legitimists defend traditional family order; modern royalists vary, so a low-confidence inference.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: The dynastic principle that Chambord's manifesto affirms links the present to the historic kingdom, but the sources do not claim continuity from ancient origins; the lean is toward continuity through the crown.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: Legitimists read politics as a Catholic counter-revolutionary struggle, while Orleanists and Bonapartists do not; the strands split.

economy-in-majority-hands.rationale: Action Francaise was hostile to minorities in economic life, but Orleanists and Bonapartists were not, so the strands split.

local-essentials-public.rationale: No shared royalist position on public services; the pro-business Orleanist and Catholic social strands differ.

second-chamber.rationale: The 1830 Charter set up a Chamber of Peers beside the elected Chamber, and the historic royalist model is bicameral, though Action Francaise disliked parliaments. None of the cited sources takes up this question, so the answer is an inference.

confederal-coordination.rationale: Chambord urged decentralisation and Action Francaise a federal monarchy, but neither describes confederations without governing power.

anonymous-payments.rationale: No shared royalist view; Orleanist liberals and a sovereign state tradition differ on financial privacy.

online-anonymity.rationale: No shared royalist view; the left-wing NAR and authoritarian Action Francaise would differ.

person-over-state.rationale: Catholic Legitimists stress the person and natural limits on power, while Bonapartists and Action Francaise stress the state; strands split.

spiritual-nature.rationale: The Throne-and-Altar tradition and Legitimist Catholicism affirm a spiritual dimension of politics, though Orleanists and the NAR are less committed. None of the cited sources takes up this question, so the answer is an inference.

regional-powers-revocable.rationale: Chambord favoured local liberties, and Action Francaise a federal monarchy, but royalists do not agree on whether regional powers are revocable.

racial-pride.rationale: Royalists celebrate national and dynastic heritage, but racial pride is not a shared doctrine and Maurrassian nationalism is excluded from this profile.

foreign-partition-plot.rationale: Action Francaise saw foreign and internal enemies weakening France, but other strands do not share that frame, so adherents are split.

free-public-college.rationale: The strands split: Nouvelle Action Royaliste leans to public provision and the Orleanist and Legitimist traditions to private or Church schooling.

women-distinct-values.rationale: Legitimist traditionalists stress distinct sexual roles while the NAR and Orleanists are closer to liberal equality, so the strands are split.

collective-bargaining.rationale: Strands split: Action Francaise favoured corporations, the NAR is pro-labour, Orleanists were liberal on contracts.

restructure-world-economy.rationale: Split: the anti-neoliberal NAR may favour it, other strands never took it up.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Royalists want to restore historic institutions and continuity, not dismantle bureaucracy, army and courts.

sacred-nation.rationale: Legitimists and Action Francaise treat France as an enduring historic community across generations, rooted in dynasty and Church.

religions-one-truth.rationale: Legitimists want a Catholic kingship while Orleanists and the Nouvelle Action Royaliste accept religious freedom, so the strands split.

one-language-many-names.rationale: No shared royalist position; Action Francaise favoured regional federalism while others stressed national linguistic unity.

environment-over-liberty.rationale: No shared position: the pro-business Orleanist tradition and the interventionist left royalists would answer differently.

mandatory-sentences.rationale: Royalist strands share no penal doctrine; the Charter leaves justice to independent judges while authoritarian strands favour firmness.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: Legitimists want a Catholic kingship while Orleanists backed a liberal Charter that recognised several faiths, so the strands split.

premarital-sex.rationale: Catholic Legitimists disapprove while liberal Orleanists and the left-wing NAR do not; the strands split.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: Legitimists are traditionally Catholic while Orleanists and Bonapartists were not literalist; the strands are split.

indirect-election.rationale: Split: Bonapartists favour plebiscites and Orleanists restricted franchise, while Legitimists favour hereditary rule, so no common answer on selection by delegates.

national-church-status.rationale: Legitimists favour Catholicism's privileged place, while Orleanists and Bonapartists accepted religious pluralism under the Charter and Concordat; strands are split.

disputed-territory-plebiscite.rationale: Split: Bonapartists made plebiscites central to their legitimacy, while Legitimists rely on dynastic right rather than popular votes.

protect-kin-minorities.rationale: Chambord's manifesto speaks of national unity and Alsace-Lorraine, but modern royalists do not share a doctrine on kin minorities abroad; strands split.

targeted-social-spending.rationale: Strands split: the left-wing NAR favours broad public provision, while Orleanist tradition leaned toward limited, targeted help; no shared doctrine.

bypass-parties-groups.rationale: Royalists see parties as divisive and the king as above them, but Legitimists and Orleanists keep intermediate bodies and local liberties (Chambord), while Bonapartists favour plebiscites; split, leaning against bypassing.

no-denominational-politics.rationale: Legitimists want a Catholic kingship while Orleanists and Bonapartists accepted religious pluralism under the Charter and Concordat; strands split.

wife-divorce-without-consent.rationale: Divorce law is not a royalist doctrine; Legitimists follow Catholic teaching against divorce, while Orleanists and Bonapartists accepted civil divorce; split.

notes: Strands split on most questions outside the monarchy itself. Action Francaise (and the older Legitimists) answer the far-right and Catholic-integralist way on democracy, parliament, minorities and the Church; Nouvelle Action Royaliste is democratic, Keynesian and anti-racist; classic Orleanists were liberal and pro-business; Bonapartists add plebiscites and a centralised state. The previous version of this audit followed Maurras alone and duplicated integral-nationalism; its candidate statement on the French Revolution (merged as restore-past-order) is an Action Francaise and Legitimist position that NAR, which accepts 1789, does not share.
